title: Triangles
notes: Similar figures: same shape, not necessarily same size. All congruent figures are similar, but similar figures need not be congruent.

Two polygons (same number of sides) are similar if: (i) corresponding angles are equal AND (ii) corresponding sides are in the same ratio. BOTH conditions needed -- angles-equal alone or sides-proportional alone is not enough.

Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales Theorem / Theorem 6.1): If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle intersecting the other two sides at distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
Converse of BPT (Theorem 6.2): If a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, it is parallel to the third side.

Similarity criteria for triangles: AAA (all 3 angles equal), AA (just 2 angles equal is enough since the 3rd is automatically equal), SSS (all 3 sides proportional), SAS (one angle equal + the two sides forming it proportional).
RHS Similarity Criterion (Note to Reader): in two right triangles, if the hypotenuse and one side of one are proportional to the hypotenuse and one side of the other, the triangles are similar.
Common proof strategy: prove two triangles similar first (using AA usually), then use the property that corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional to derive the required relation.

formulas.name: Basic Proportionality Theorem
formulas.formula: If DE || BC in triangle ABC (D on AB, E on AC): AD/DB = AE/EC
formulas.use: Finding unknown segment lengths when a line is parallel to one side.

formulas.name: AA Similarity
formulas.formula: 2 angles of one triangle = 2 angles of another -> triangles similar

formulas.name: SSS Similarity
formulas.formula: AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD -> triangle ABC ~ triangle DEF
formulas.use: When all three side ratios are given/computable.

formulas.name: SAS Similarity
formulas.formula: One angle equal + including sides proportional -> triangles similar
formulas.use: When one angle and its two arms' ratios are known.

formulas.name: Indirect height/distance (shadow method)
formulas.use: Classic tower/pole shadow problems using similar triangles.

examples.question: Are a square and a rhombus similar even though sides are proportional?
examples.solution: No -- proportional sides alone isn't enough; corresponding angles must also be equal. A square has all 90-degree angles, a rhombus generally doesn't, so they're not similar despite equal side ratios.

examples.question: A vertical pole 6m casts a 4m shadow. At the same time a tower casts a 28m shadow. Find the tower's height.
examples.solution: Using similar triangles (pole/shadow ratio = tower/shadow ratio): 6/4 = h/28, so h = 6*28/4 = 42m.
